structured_notes.title: Mark Weiser's Ubiquitous Computing Device Categories (Tabs, Pads, Boards)
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Mark Weiser's Classification of Ubiquitous Smart Devices
A **smart device** is digital, active, computer-networked, user-reconfigurable, and capable of operating autonomously.

| Category | Scale / Dimension | Usage Characteristic | Examples |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Tabs** | Centimeter-sized ($\text{cm}$) | Accompanied or wearable devices carried by a single user | Smartphones, smart cards, wearables |
| **Pads** | Decimeter-sized ($\text{dm}$) | Hand-held dispositivos used temporarily and passed around | Laptops, tablets, e-readers |
| **Boards** | Meter-sized ($\text{m}$) | Shared interactive display surfaces in rooms | Vertical smart boards, horizontal surface computers |
summary_bullets: Tabs = Centimeter-sized wearable/accompanied devices (smartphones, smart cards).
Pads = Decimeter-sized hand-held devices (laptops, tablets).
Boards = Meter-sized interactive multi-user displays (smart boards).

structured_notes.title: Feature Phone vs. Smartphone & Mobile Device Characteristics
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Feature Phones vs. Smartphones
- **Feature Phone**: Runs on proprietary firmware with limited third-party platform extensibility.
- **Smartphone**: Runs an open and complete Mobile Operating System (Android, iOS) tightly integrated with high-resolution touchscreens, GPS, Wi-Fi/mobile broadband, and third-party SDK APIs.
- **Core Mobile Characteristics**: Context awareness, intermittent resource connectivity, and a **locus of control** residing inside the smart device.
summary_bullets: Feature phones rely on closed/proprietary firmware.
Smartphones run complete mobile OS platforms supporting native SDKs.
Mobile apps must handle intermittent network access and context awareness.

structured_notes.title: Android Software Stack & ART / Dalvik Runtime
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Android Architecture Layers (Bottom to Top)
1. **Linux Kernel**: Hardware abstraction drivers (display, camera, binder IPC, power management).
2. **Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL)**: Standard interfaces exposing hardware capabilities.
3. **Native C/C++ Libraries & Android Runtime (ART)**: Executes `.dex` (Dalvik Executable) bytecode using Ahead-of-Time (AOT) and Just-in-Time (JIT) compilation.
4. **Java API Framework**: Activity Manager, Window Manager, Content Providers, View System.
5. **System Apps**: Dialer, SMS, Browser, and user-installed apps.
summary_bullets: Java/Kotlin source compiles to .class, then packages into .dex (Dalvik Executable) bytecode.
ART (Android Runtime) replaces legacy Dalvik VM using AOT/JIT compilation for lower battery/CPU overhead.
Linux Kernel handles low-level memory, process threading, and Binder IPC.

structured_notes.title: Android Activity Lifecycle Callbacks & State Transitions
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Activity Lifecycle Order
- **Launch to Foreground**: `onCreate()` $\rightarrow$ `onStart()` $\rightarrow$ `onResume()` (Activity is visible and interactive).
- **Partially Obscured** (e.g., dialog overlays): `onPause()`.
- **Fully Hidden / Home Pressed**: `onPause()` $\rightarrow$ `onStop()`.
- **Returning from Stopped to Foreground**: `onRestart()` $\rightarrow$ `onStart()` $\rightarrow$ `onResume()`.
- **Configuration Change (Screen Rotation)**: By default destroys and recreates the Activity (`onPause()` $\rightarrow$ `onStop()` $\rightarrow$ `onDestroy()` $\rightarrow$ `onCreate()`), saving transient UI state via `onSaveInstanceState(Bundle)`.
summary_bullets: onCreate() initializes layout (setContentView) once per instance.
onResume() / onPause() bracket active foreground user interaction.
Screen rotation triggers onDestroy() -> onCreate() unless handled via ViewModel or configChanges.

structured_notes.title: Explicit vs. Implicit Intents & Intent Filters
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Android Intents Comparison
| Feature | Explicit Intent | Implicit Intent |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Target Specification** | Specifies exact class name (`new Intent(this, DetailActivity.class)`) | Declares general `Action`, `Data URI`, and `Category` (`Intent.ACTION_VIEW`) |
| **Resolution Mechanism** | Direct intra-app component invocation | Resolved by Android `PackageManager` matching `<intent-filter>` declarations in `AndroidManifest.xml` |
| **Primary Use Case** | Navigating between screens inside your own app | Delegating actions to external apps (Browser, Camera, Dialer, Share sheet) |
summary_bullets: Explicit Intents name the exact target Component/Class.
Implicit Intents declare an Action + URI and rely on Manifest <intent-filter> matching.
An Intent Filter must match Action, Data (URI/MIME type), and Category (DEFAULT).

structured_notes.title: startActivityForResult / ActivityResultLauncher Two-Way Data Passing
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Passing Data Between Activities
- **Forward Passing**: `intent.putExtra("KEY", value)` read via `getIntent().getStringExtra("KEY")`.
- **Returning Result to Caller**: The child Activity packs data into a return `Intent`, calls `setResult(Activity.RESULT_OK, resultIntent)`, and invokes `finish()`.
summary_bullets: Use putExtra() / Bundle to pass primitives, Strings, or Parcelable objects.
Child Activity must call setResult(RESULT_OK, dataIntent) BEFORE calling finish().

structured_notes.title: Android Services: Started Service vs. Bound Service & Threading
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Android Service Types & Main Thread Rule
- **Crucial Threading Rule**: A `Service` runs on the **Main (UI) Thread** of its hosting process by default! Blocking network/CPU work inside `onStartCommand()` without a worker thread causes an **ANR (Application Not Responding)** crash after ~5 seconds.
- **Started Service (`startService`)**: Runs indefinitely in background until `stopSelf()` or `stopService()` is called. Entry callback: `onStartCommand()`.
- **Bound Service (`bindService`)**: Client-server interface allowing components to bind, send requests, and receive responses via `IBinder`. Entry callback: `onBind()`.
summary_bullets: Services run on the UI/Main thread by default—always offload heavy I/O to background threads/coroutines.
Started Services use startService() -> onStartCommand() and run even after the caller unbinds.
Bound Services use bindService() -> onBind() returning an IBinder interface and stop when all clients unbind.

structured_notes.title: Service Restart Policies: START_STICKY vs. START_NOT_STICKY vs. START_REDELIVER_INTENT
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### `onStartCommand()` Return Constants
| Return Flag | OS Behavior After Low-Memory Process Kill | Intent Passed on Recreate |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `START_NOT_STICKY` | Does **not** recreate the Service unless pending start calls exist | N/A |
| `START_STICKY` | Recreates the Service and calls `onStartCommand()` | `null` Intent (good for music players/long-running pollers) |
| `START_REDELIVER_INTENT` | Recreates the Service and calls `onStartCommand()` | Redelivers the **last original Intent** (good for file downloads/transactional jobs) |
summary_bullets: START_STICKY restarts service with a null Intent.
START_NOT_STICKY does not restart automatically.
START_REDELIVER_INTENT restarts service and passes the exact original Intent.

structured_notes.title: Broadcast Receivers & Content Providers
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### BroadcastReceivers & ContentProviders
- **`BroadcastReceiver`**: Responds to system-wide or app-wide publish-subscribe announcements (e.g., `ACTION_BOOT_COMPLETED`, battery low, connectivity changes) via `onReceive(Context, Intent)`.
- **`ContentProvider`**: Manages access to a structured central repository of data across process boundaries using `ContentResolver` and `content://authority/path` URIs.
summary_bullets: BroadcastReceiver implements onReceive(Context, Intent) and must complete quickly (<10s).
ContentProvider shares structured data across different applications securely via URI permissions.

structured_notes.title: Android Local Storage: SharedPreferences vs. SQLiteOpenHelper
structured_notes.content_markdown:
### Android Data Persistence Options
- **`SharedPreferences`**: Stores lightweight primitive key-value pairs (`boolean`, `int`, `String`) in an XML file inside private app storage. `apply()` writes asynchronously to disk; `commit()` writes synchronously and blocks the calling thread.
- **`SQLiteOpenHelper`**: Manages relational SQLite database creation (`onCreate(SQLiteDatabase db)`) and schema version migrations (`onUpgrade(SQLiteDatabase db, int oldVersion, int newVersion)`).
summary_bullets: SharedPreferences Editor.apply() is asynchronous (in-memory immediate, disk async); commit() is synchronous.
SQLiteOpenHelper calls onCreate() only when the DB file is first created, and onUpgrade() when DATABASE_VERSION increments.

questions.question_text:
According to Mark Weiser's foundational categorization of ubiquitous computing smart devices, how are **Tabs**, **Pads**, and **Boards** classified by their physical scale and usage?

| Category | Physical Scale | Typical Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **I** | Centimeter-sized ($\text{cm}$) | Smartphones, Smart Cards |
| **II** | Decimeter-sized ($\text{dm}$) | Laptops, Handheld Tablets |
| **III** | Meter-sized ($\text{m}$) | Vertical Smart Boards, Surface Computers |

options.label: A
options.text: I = Pads, II = Tabs, III = Boards

options.label: B
options.text: I = Tabs, II = Pads, III = Boards

options.label: C
options.text: I = Boards, II = Pads, III = Tabs

options.label: D
options.text: I = Tabs, II = Boards, III = Pads

questions.explanation:
- **Why B is correct**: Mark Weiser categorized ubiquitous computing devices by physical scale: **Tabs** are centimeter-sized accompanied/wearable devices (smartphones, smart cards); **Pads** are decimeter-sized hand-held devices (laptops, tablets); and **Boards** are meter-sized interactive display surfaces.
- **Why A is incorrect**: Reverses Tabs and Pads.
- **Why C and D are incorrect**: Misassign meter-sized Boards to centimeter or decimeter scales.

questions.question_text: Which statement accurately distinguishes a **Smartphone** from a traditional **Feature Phone** in mobile computing architecture?

options.label: A
options.text: Feature phones run open, complete mobile operating systems, whereas smartphones rely exclusively on closed proprietary firmware.

options.label: B
options.text: Smartphones provide an open and complete mobile operating system tightly integrated with third-party SDKs, sensors, and broadband networking, whereas feature phones use proprietary firmware with limited platform extensibility.

options.label: C
options.text: Feature phones maintain the locus of control on remote cloud mainframes, whereas smartphones cannot execute local application services.

options.label: D
options.text: Smartphones cannot operate autonomously when disconnected from a wireless local area network.

questions.explanation:
- **Why B is correct**: A smartphone combines PDA, media, GPS, and web capabilities on top of an open and complete mobile OS (such as Android) supporting native third-party application development, while a feature phone runs proprietary firmware with restricted platform APIs.
- **Why A is incorrect**: Reverses the definitions of smartphone and feature phone.
- **Why C and D are incorrect**: Smart mobile devices hold an internal locus of control and can execute local services autonomously despite intermittent connectivity.

questions.question_text: During the Android build and execution process, how is Java/Kotlin source code compiled and executed on a modern Android device?

options.label: A
options.text: Source code is compiled directly into native x86 Windows `.exe` binaries and executed by the BIOS.

options.label: B
options.text: Source code is compiled into `.class` bytecode, converted into Dalvik Executable (`.dex`) files, packaged into an `.apk`/`.aab`, and executed by the Android Runtime (ART).

options.label: C
options.text: Raw `.java` source files are uploaded uncompiled into the `.apk` and interpreted line-by-line by the Linux kernel.

options.label: D
options.text: Bytecode is executed inside a standard desktop Oracle JVM without any `.dex` transformation.

questions.explanation:
- **Why B is correct**: Android compiles `.java`/`.kt` files to JVM `.class` files, uses the `d8`/`r8` compiler to convert them into compact `.dex` (Dalvik Executable) bytecode optimized for memory-constrained devices, packages them into an `.apk`, and runs them on the Android Runtime (ART).
- **Why A, C, and D are incorrect**: Android does not use `.exe` binaries, uncompiled source interpretation in the kernel, or standard desktop `.class` files at runtime.

questions.question_text: An Android `ExamActivity` is currently visible and actively receiving user touch input in the foreground. The user then receives a semi-transparent system permission dialog (or multi-window overlay) that partially obscures `ExamActivity` so it loses focus but remains partially visible on screen. Which lifecycle callback is invoked immediately?

options.label: A
options.text: onDestroy()

options.label: B
options.text: onStop() followed immediately by onDestroy()

options.label: C
options.text: onPause() only (without calling onStop() while the Activity remains partially visible)

options.label: D
options.text: onRestart()

questions.explanation:
- **Why C is correct**: When an Activity loses foreground focus but remains partially visible behind a transparent/dialog Activity, Android invokes `onPause()`. `onStop()` is only invoked when the Activity becomes completely hidden from view.
- **Why A and B are incorrect**: `onStop()` and `onDestroy()` are not called while the Activity is still visible on screen.
- **Why D is incorrect**: `onRestart()` is called only when transitioning from a stopped (`onStop()`) state back to `onStart()`.

options.label: A
options.text: 30, because Android preserves all private member variables across device rotations automatically.

options.label: B
options.text: 0, because a screen orientation change triggers a configuration change that destroys the current Activity instance (onPause -> onStop -> onDestroy) and creates a new instance (onCreate), resetting currentScore to 0 unless saved via onSaveInstanceState or a ViewModel.

options.label: C
options.text: 30, because onCreate() is only called once when the application process first boots.

options.label: D
options.text: The app crashes with a NullPointerException because Activities cannot be rotated without a Service.

questions.explanation:
- **Why B is correct**: By default, rotating the screen is a runtime configuration change that destroys the existing `QuizActivity` instance and instantiates a brand-new `QuizActivity` (`onCreate()`). Because `currentScore` is an instance field and `onSaveInstanceState(Bundle)` / `ViewModel` was not used, `currentScore` resets to `0`.
- **Why A and C are incorrect**: Instance variables on an `Activity` are wiped when the instance is destroyed and recreated.
- **Why D is incorrect**: Rotation does not require a `Service`.

options.label: A
options.text: intentA is an Implicit Intent; intentB is an Explicit Intent.

options.label: B
options.text: intentA is an Explicit Intent; intentB is an Implicit Intent.

options.label: C
options.text: Both intentA and intentB are Implicit Intents.

options.label: D
options.text: intentA is a Broadcast Intent; intentB is a Bound Service Intent.

questions.explanation:
- **Why B is correct**: `intentA` explicitly specifies the exact target component class (`ResultActivity.class`), making it an **Explicit Intent**. `intentB` specifies only an action (`ACTION_VIEW`) and data URI (`https://...`), leaving Android to resolve capable browser apps via `<intent-filter>`, making it an **Implicit Intent**.
- **Why A, C, and D are incorrect**: Confuse component-targeted explicit intents with action-resolved implicit intents.

questions.question_text: An application declares an `<activity>` in `AndroidManifest.xml` with an `<intent-filter>` so other apps can launch it using an implicit `startActivity(intent)` call (without adding explicit categories to the Intent in Java code). Which `<category>` **must** be included inside the `<intent-filter>` for `startActivity()` to resolve this Activity?

options.label: A
options.text: android.intent.category.LAUNCHER

options.label: B
options.text: android.intent.category.DEFAULT

options.label: C
options.text: android.intent.category.HOME

options.label: D
options.text: android.intent.category.BROWSABLE only

questions.explanation:
- **Why B is correct**: When `startActivity()` or `startActivityForResult()` is called with an implicit `Intent`, Android automatically attaches `CATEGORY_DEFAULT` (`android.intent.category.DEFAULT`) to the Intent. Any Activity wishing to receive implicit Intents must therefore declare `<category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />` in its `<intent-filter>`.
- **Why A is incorrect**: `CATEGORY_LAUNCHER` places an icon in the device's app launcher drawer.
- **Why C and D are incorrect**: `HOME` is for home screen replacements, and `BROWSABLE` alone without `DEFAULT` will fail standard implicit `startActivity` resolution.

questions.question_text: `CourseCatalogActivity` launches `FilterSelectionActivity` expecting the user's selected department code back. Inside `FilterSelectionActivity`, which sequence of calls correctly sends `"IT"` back to the calling Activity and closes `FilterSelectionActivity`?

options.label: A
B
C
options.text:
startActivity(new Intent("IT"));
System.exit(0);

options.label: D
options.text:
onDestroy();
return "IT";

questions.explanation:
- **Why A is correct**: To return data to a parent Activity, the child Activity creates a result `Intent`, attaches extras via `putExtra()`, calls `setResult(Activity.RESULT_OK, data)`, and then calls `finish()` to pop itself off the back stack.
- **Why B is incorrect**: Calls `finish()` before `setResult()` and sets `RESULT_CANCELED`.
- **Why C and D are incorrect**: `System.exit(0)` kills the whole Linux process, and `onDestroy()` is a lifecycle callback, not a method used to return results.

options.label: A
options.text: The download completes smoothly in the background because every Android Service automatically creates its own separate background thread.

options.label: B
options.text: The UI freezes and Android triggers an ANR (Application Not Responding) dialog because a Service runs on the application's Main (UI) thread by default.

options.label: C
options.text: The code fails to compile because onBind() returns null.

options.label: D
options.text: The download is automatically converted into a BroadcastReceiver by the OS.

questions.explanation:
- **Why B is correct**: A common Android exam trap is assuming `Service` runs on a background thread. By default, a `Service` runs on the hosting process's **Main (UI) thread**. Executing a 30-second synchronous network download inside `onStartCommand()` blocks the UI thread and causes both a `NetworkOnMainThreadException` and an **ANR (Application Not Responding)** timeout.
- **Why A is incorrect**: `Service` does not spawn a worker thread automatically.
- **Why C is incorrect**: Returning `null` from `onBind()` is standard for a pure Started (unbound) Service.
- **Why D is incorrect**: Services are never converted into BroadcastReceivers.

questions.question_text: What is the key architectural difference between a **Started Service** (`startService()`) and a **Bound Service** (`bindService()`) in Android?

options.label: A
options.text: A Started Service continues running in the background indefinitely until explicitly stopped (even if the starting Activity is destroyed), whereas a Bound Service runs only as long as at least one client component is bound to it via IBinder.

options.label: B
options.text: A Started Service requires a visible user interface layout, whereas a Bound Service does not.

options.label: C
options.text: A Bound Service cannot return values or expose methods to an Activity, whereas a Started Service returns an IBinder in onStartCommand().

options.label: D
options.text: A Started Service is destroyed immediately when the user rotates the screen.

questions.explanation:
- **Why A is correct**: A Started Service (`onStartCommand`) has an independent lifecycle and stays alive until `stopSelf()` or `stopService()` is called. A Bound Service (`onBind`) acts as a server in a client-server relationship via an `IBinder` and is automatically destroyed by the OS when all bound clients call `unbindService()`.
- **Why B is incorrect**: Neither Service type has a UI layout.
- **Why C is incorrect**: `onBind()` returns the `IBinder`, not `onStartCommand()`.
- **Why D is incorrect**: Started Services survive Activity configuration changes.

questions.question_text: An Android Service is processing an offline exam submission payload passed inside the `Intent` argument of `onStartCommand(Intent intent, int flags, int startId)`. If the Android OS temporarily kills the Service process due to low memory before the job finishes, which return constant guarantees the OS will recreate the Service **and** re-pass the exact same non-null `Intent`?

options.label: A
options.text: Service.START_NOT_STICKY

options.label: B
options.text: Service.START_STICKY

options.label: C
options.text: Service.START_REDELIVER_INTENT

options.label: D
options.text: Service.BIND_AUTO_CREATE

questions.explanation:
- **Why C is correct**: `START_REDELIVER_INTENT` instructs the system to recreate the Service after a low-memory kill and call `onStartCommand()` with the last `Intent` that was delivered to the Service before it was killed.
- **Why A is incorrect**: `START_NOT_STICKY` does not recreate the Service at all.
- **Why B is incorrect**: `START_STICKY` recreates the Service, but passes a `null` Intent to `onStartCommand()`.
- **Why D is incorrect**: `BIND_AUTO_CREATE` is a flag for `bindService()`, not a return value of `onStartCommand()`.

questions.question_text: Which of the four fundamental Android application components is specifically designed to listen for and respond to system-wide or application-wide event announcements (such as `ACTION_BATTERY_LOW` or network connectivity changes)?

options.label: A
options.text: ContentProvider

options.label: B
options.text: BroadcastReceiver

options.label: C
options.text: RecyclerView.Adapter

options.label: D
options.text: SQLiteOpenHelper

questions.explanation:
- **Why B is correct**: `BroadcastReceiver` is the core Android component that subscribes to system or custom broadcast `Intent`s and handles them inside `onReceive(Context context, Intent intent)`.
- **Why A is incorrect**: `ContentProvider` shares structured data across apps.
- **Why C and D are incorrect**: `RecyclerView.Adapter` and `SQLiteOpenHelper` are helper classes, not one of the four fundamental Android components (`Activity`, `Service`, `BroadcastReceiver`, `ContentProvider`).

questions.question_text: An Android app needs to read contacts stored by the system Contacts application. Which class and URI scheme does the client app use to query the Contacts `ContentProvider`?

options.label: A
options.text: getContentResolver().query(...) using a content://authority/path URI

options.label: B
options.text: getSharedPreferences() using an http://localhost/contacts URI

options.label: C
options.text: sendBroadcast() using a file:///system/contacts.db URI

options.label: D
options.text: SQLiteDatabase.openDatabase() directly on the Contacts app's private data folder

questions.explanation:
- **Why A is correct**: Applications never access another app's `ContentProvider` or private SQLite file directly. Instead, they call `Context.getContentResolver().query(...)` passing a `content://` URI (`ContactsContract.Contacts.CONTENT_URI`).
- **Why B, C, and D are incorrect**: Android Linux user-ID sandboxing forbids direct file access (`file://`) to another app's private SQLite database.

options.label: A
options.text: apply() encrypts the XML file with AES-256, whereas commit() stores plaintext.

options.label: B
options.text: apply() updates the in-memory SharedPreferences immediately and writes to disk asynchronously on a background thread without blocking the UI thread, whereas commit() performs a synchronous disk write that can block the UI thread.

options.label: C
options.text: commit() only saves data in RAM and loses changes when the app closes, whereas apply() writes to SQLite.

options.label: D
options.text: apply() returns a boolean success status synchronously, whereas commit() returns void.

questions.explanation:
- **Why B is correct**: `apply()` mutates the in-memory `SharedPreferences` object immediately and schedules an asynchronous disk write, preventing UI jank/ANRs on the main thread. `commit()` blocks the calling thread until the physical disk write finishes and returns a `boolean` result.
- **Why A and C are incorrect**: Both write to the same XML backing file.
- **Why D is incorrect**: `commit()` returns `boolean`, whereas `apply()` has a `void` return type.

options.label: A
options.text: Immediately inside the ExamDbHelper constructor before any database access is requested.

options.label: B
options.text: The first time getWritableDatabase() or getReadableDatabase() is called, Android detects that the stored database version (1) is lower than DATABASE_VERSION (2) and invokes onUpgrade(db, 1, 2) inside a transaction.

options.label: C
options.text: onCreate(db) is called again automatically on every app launch regardless of version number.

options.label: D
options.text: Never, unless the developer manually invokes dbHelper.onUpgrade() inside MainActivity.onCreate().

questions.explanation:
- **Why B is correct**: `SQLiteOpenHelper` is lazy: the constructor does not open or migrate the database. When `getWritableDatabase()` or `getReadableDatabase()` is first called, Android opens the database file, compares its `PRAGMA user_version` (`1`) with `DATABASE_VERSION` (`2`), and executes `onUpgrade(db, 1, 2)`.
- **Why A is incorrect**: The constructor only stores metadata references.
- **Why C is incorrect**: `onCreate()` only runs once when the database file does not exist yet.
- **Why D is incorrect**: The framework calls `onUpgrade()` automatically upon opening the database.
